about: Outflows from stars (O3b, gap R26): a cool giant's dusty wind and a young star's jets, published as nebulae for the renderer to draw.

references: Schröder, K.-P. and Cuntz, M. 2005, A new version of Reimers' law of mass loss based on a physical approach, ApJ 630, L73: Ṁ = η L R / M (T_eff / 4000 K)^3.5 (1 + g_sun / (4300 g)) in solar masses a year with η = 8e-14, for cool giants and supergiants. doi:10.1086/491579

equation.name: How fast a cool giant sheds its outer layers
equation.formula:
l = L / Lsun
r = R / Rsun
mm = M / Msun
g = G * M / (R * R)
gs = G * Msun / (Rsun * Rsun)
q = T / t0
Md = eta * l * r / mm * q^(7/2) * (1 + gs / (gfac * g)) * Msun / yr

Md.name: mass the star sheds each second

source.text: Schröder, K.-P. and Cuntz, M. 2005, ApJ 630, L73

explain.curious: A swollen red giant holds its outer layers so loosely that its own light and pulsing blow them away, a little every year, building a slow wind around it.
explain.science: Reimers-type mass loss with a chromospheric correction for temperature and gravity, calibrated on globular cluster horizontal branches.

Tc.source: Höfner and Olofsson 2018, section 4: silicate and carbon grains condense near 1000 to 1500 K

kap.source: a flux-mean dust opacity per mass of gas, of the order Höfner and Olofsson 2018 give for dust-driven winds (fudge F57)

checks.says: mass-loss rate must be zero or more, got {}

references: Höfner, S. and Olofsson, H. 2018, Mass loss of stars on the asymptotic giant branch, A&ARv 26, 1, section 4: dust forms where the radiative equilibrium temperature falls to the condensation temperature, R_c = (R/2)(T_eff/T_c)^((4+p)/2), p about 1 for small grains; dust drives the wind. doi:10.1007/s00159-017-0106-5

equation.name: Where a giant's wind turns to dust, and how much light the dust takes and gives again
equation.formula:
q = T / Tc
rc = R / 2 * q^(5/2)
tau = kap * Md / (4 * pi * v * rc)
Ld = L * (1 - exp(-tau))
Td = Tc

Md.name: mass the star sheds each second

kap.name: dust's opacity per kilogram of gas

rc.name: distance from the star where dust forms

tau.name: how thick the dust is to starlight, looking out

Ld.name: starlight the dust takes in and glows out again in the infrared

source.text: Höfner, S. and Olofsson, H. 2018, A&ARv 26, 1

explain.curious: Some way out from a red giant its wind cools enough for soot and sand-like grains to form. That dust hides some of the star and glows warm in the infrared.
explain.science: Condensation radius from radiative equilibrium of grains with p = 1; radial optical depth of a steady wind from the condensation radius out; absorbed light re-emitted.

f.source: Hartigan, Edwards and Ghandour 1995: jets carry about a tenth of the accretion rate

share.source: share of a jet's power given off as light in its shocks (fudge F57)

checks.says: accretion rate must be zero or more, got {}

references: Hartigan, P., Edwards, S. and Ghandour, L. 1995, Disk accretion and mass loss from young stars, ApJ 452, 736: young stars put about a tenth of what they accrete into their jets. doi:10.1086/176343

Bally, J. 2016, Protostellar outflows, ARA&A 54, 491: jets leave at speeds near the escape speed from where they are launched in the inner disc, a few hundred km/s, and are knotted by episodic accretion. doi:10.1146/annurev-astro-081915-023341
atoms.shown: Ṁ_j = f Ṁ_acc,  v_j = √(2GM/r_l),  P_j = ½ Ṁ_j v_j²,  L_s = s P_j

equation.name: How strong and fast a young star's jets are
equation.formula:
Mj = f * Ma
vj = sqrt(2 * G * M / rl)
Pj = Mj * vj * vj / 2
Ls = share * Pj

Ma.name: mass falling onto the young star each second

rl.name: distance from the star where the jet is launched from its disc

f.name: share of the accreted mass the jets carry away

share.name: share of the jet's power its shocks give off as light

Mj.name: mass both jets carry away each second

Ls.name: light the jets' shocks give off

source.text: Hartigan, P., Edwards, S. and Ghandour, L. 1995, ApJ 452, 736

explain.curious: A star still feeding from its disc fires two thin jets out of its poles at hundreds of kilometres a second. Where they hit slower gas they glow red.
explain.science: Jet mass flux as a fixed share of accretion; launch speed at the escape speed from the inner disc; shock luminosity as a share of the mechanical power.
